summary: Specifies how DNS resource records are named and structured so clients can discover services. Given a service type and a domain, a client can find a list of named instances of that service using standard DNS queries. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Domain Name System (DNS)-based Service Discovery (DNS-SD) lets a client find named services in a domain using ordinary DNS queries. Records provide a list of choices, the host and port for each choice, and optional details.

subtitle: How ordinary DNS records let clients browse for services and find the host and port of a chosen instance.

tldr.problem: Clients need to discover named instances of a service in a domain and learn how to contact a chosen instance.
tldr.mechanism: A PTR query lists service instance names; SRV records give the target host and port, and TXT records carry service-specific details.
tldr.outcome: DNS-SD reuses existing DNS record types and works with Multicast DNS and unicast DNS. RFC 6763 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8553.

today: RFC 6763 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8553. The RFC describes use with Multicast DNS in RFC 6762 and conventional unicast DNS.

sections.title: The DNS-Based Discovery Model
sections.content:
DNS-based Service Discovery (DNS-SD) uses DNS resource records to list named instances of a service. It defines no new DNS message format, operation code, response code, or resource-record type. A service instance uses an SRV record to identify its target host and port, and a TXT record for additional service-specific information.

A client discovers instances with a PTR query for a service type and domain. The same naming and record conventions work with Multicast DNS on a local link and with ordinary unicast DNS. Multicast DNS can support configuration-free operation; unicast deployments usually need domain and update configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS-SD uses existing DNS records to help a client find a service by type and name. It works with local multicast queries and with regular DNS servers.

sections.title: Service Names and Browsing
sections.content:
A PTR query for <Service>.<Domain> returns zero or more service instance names of the form <Instance>.<Service>.<Domain>. The instance part is user-visible text encoded as one DNS label. It may include spaces, punctuation, and Unicode characters, but not ASCII control characters; DNS limits a label to 63 octets.

The service portion consists of an underscore-prefixed service name followed by _tcp for TCP applications or _udp for other transports. The domain can be local. for link-local Multicast DNS or a unicast domain. If software joins the name parts into one string, it must preserve label boundaries, including dots that are literal characters in the instance name.
sections.plainLanguage: A browse query returns readable names for the available services. The name has separate parts for the instance, service type, and domain.

sections.title: Finding the Host and Port
sections.content:
After a user selects an instance, the client queries for its SRV and TXT records. The SRV record gives the target host and port. The TXT record carries additional details defined for that service type.

If several SRV records are returned, clients must prefer lower-numbered priorities and select among equal-priority servers randomly in proportion to their weights. When one SRV record describes an instance, its priority and weight should both be zero.
sections.plainLanguage: After a person chooses a service name, its service-location record tells the client which host and port to contact. A text record can provide more details needed by that service.

sections.title: TXT Records for Service Details
sections.content:
Each DNS-SD service must have a TXT record with the same name as its SRV record, even when the TXT record contains no additional information. A TXT record contains one or more length-prefixed strings. DNS-SD uses each string for one key/value pair, such as paper=A4; a string without an equals sign is a present key with no value.

Keys use printable US-ASCII other than the equals sign, are case-insensitive, and should be no more than nine characters. Unknown keys must be ignored. Duplicate keys should not be sent; clients that receive duplicates use only the first. TXT data is opaque binary data, and the RFC recommends keeping typical records to 200 bytes or less and avoiding records larger than 1300 bytes.

The host and port belong in the SRV record and must not be repeated as TXT key/value pairs. Profile authors are advised to make txtvers the first pair so clients can decide whether they understand the TXT format.
sections.plainLanguage: The TXT record stores small service details as labeled values. Clients can ignore unfamiliar labels, so a service can add fields without requiring every client to change.

sections.title: Service Types, Subtypes, and Name Coordination
sections.content:
A service name identifies what a service does as well as the protocol it uses; it is not simply the name of an underlying transport. Service names follow the registry rules referenced by the RFC: at most 15 characters, made from letters, digits, and hyphens, and containing at least one letter.

A subtype lets a client request a narrower set of instances while keeping them discoverable under the main service type. For example, a printer's web page can be listed under both _http._tcp and a printer subtype. For related protocols that offer the same kind of service, a designated flagship service name helps devices avoid assigning the same friendly instance name to different services. A placeholder SRV record reserves a name without advertising a discoverable service.

A PTR query for _services._dns-sd._udp.<Domain> can enumerate service types. The RFC notes that a unicast DNS response can contain up to 839 instances with maximum-sized instance names, though it recommends dividing very large lists into logical subdomains.
sections.plainLanguage: Service names describe the service a client can use, and subtypes let clients narrow a list. A shared naming rule also helps related services avoid claiming the same instance name.

sections.title: Publishing Records and Finding Domains
sections.content:
How PTR, SRV, and TXT records are entered into DNS is outside the RFC's scope. It gives examples such as administrator-managed zone files, DNS Update, and devices that answer Multicast DNS queries for names ending in .local..

Five reserved PTR query names help a client learn suggested browsing and registration domains: b, db, r, dr, and lb under _dns-sd._udp.<domain>. Their results are advisory. DNS responders should add related SRV, TXT, A, and AAAA records to PTR answers when appropriate, but clients must still work if those extra records are absent.
sections.plainLanguage: A network can publish service records in several ways. Special DNS queries can also suggest which domains a client should browse or use when registering services.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
DNS-SD is a convention for naming and using existing DNS records, so it adds no security requirements beyond DNS queries and updates. The RFC recommends DNSSEC when clients need authentic query results and secure updates to control which clients can change DNS records. Clients decide whether to trust additional records included in a response.

IANA manages the service-name namespace. Specifications using subtypes or flagship naming should document those names so that different services do not assign conflicting meanings.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS-based Service Discovery relies on the security mechanisms already used by the Domain Name System. Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) can help verify answers, and update permissions control who can change records.
